messages.subject: ODE branch status?
messages.body_plain:
You're having such a good and important conversation about new features that I almost hate to intrude with a specific question, but I will.

Is there any news about the status of the ODE development work?  I may have a problem where I'd like to use such a tool very soon (and I may not).  If I do, I see at least three choices:

- the ODE features that are coming in Stan

- deSolve and FME in R

- MCSim

If Stan's ODE capabilities are good enough to use and buildable by a non-expert today, I might be tempted to try it (a bit risky for me, as this is for real work, not "simply" research).  If it's not that close, I'd seek out another alternative this time around.

Thanks,

Bill

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] ODE branch status?
messages.body_plain:
We won't actually have ODE in Stan's modeling language
for a while.

You can follow the integrator branch to see how we implemented
an example using Boost's integrators.  We're working on some
other models in a private branch, and those have also worked
well.

But it's going to require C++ coding of the solver as we
did in the integration branch and then building the resulting
function into Stan.  It's not that much work, but it's completely
undocumented so far.

And there's no support for stiff equations yet.

I have no firsthand experience with deSolve/FME in R
or with MCSim.  We've been consulting with Frederic Bois,
the developer of MCSim, on the work for Stan, and we've
used some code he's written in deSolve to validate the
integrator in Stan.  But I haven't actually used MCSim
or deSolve myself.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: Stability of our code base, new vs. existing features
messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: Stability of our code base, new vs. existing features
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'll just cast a vote in favor of stability and gradually widening the
performance gap between JAGS/BUGS.

Whence my vote for stability? Python does not have JAGS or BUGS so Stan occupies
a very different position in the statistical computing ecosystem than it does in
R.

One serious suggestion: what about a long-term support release cycle like Ubuntu
that permits rapid development and experimentation in the meantime. For those
who aren't familiar with this: Ubuntu (Linux) has a very stable release every
two years that they pledge to support/fix bugs for. Between the LTS releases
they have other more experimental releases for which they do not pledge the same
kind of vigilance. This seems to work very well. It's actually a very nice
contract between developers and users. Users know that they are getting
something that might have bugs if they don't take the LTS release.

Minor point:

- Echoing Jiqiang, I don't want to support Windows on PyStan until/unless
  a Windows developer joins the PyStan team. I'd like to make this position
  explicit.

Best,

Allen

On 11/29, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It looks like we all understand each other at this point
> and just have different opinions about where Stan should
> go.
>
> Among the core developers
>
>   * Matt, Jiqiang, Allen, and Peter haven't weighed in,
>
>   * Daniel and I favor slower development with an emphasis
>     on stability and a stricter process, and
>
>   * Marcus, Ben, Michael, and Andrew favor an emphasis on
>     research and new features and a more relaxed process.
>
> Both goals make sense, so there's no "right" answer here.
>
> With such differing opinions on our goals, it's obvious
> that a consensus isn't going to work any more.
> Nominally, Andrew's in charge, but as far as I know, he's
> never even looked at the code.
>
> Assuming nobody else has anything to add at this point,
> this leaves open the question of what Marcus,
> Ben, Michael, and Andrew think the process should be.  I'm
> specifically thinking about new code and doc in terms of:
>
>   * designing
>   * prioritizing
>   * coding
>   * testing
>   * continuously integrating
>   * documenting
>   * reviewing
>   * merging
>   * releasing
>   * integrating (R, Python, etc.)
>
> An extreme answer would be to skip overall design and
> prioritization, put no requirements on testing and doc,
> shut down the continuous integration server,
> skip code review, give everyone push permission, forgo
> official releases, and leave those working on RStan
> and PyStan to fend for themselves on integration.
> I'm guessing this would inevitably lead to everyone forking the
> code and working on his (or her if any women ever join
> the team) own version.
>
> - Bob
>
> On 11/29/13, 4:16 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> >Ok, I've been hesitant to weigh in on this for a number of reasons but after Ben's post I've decided to follow suite and
> >post some high level comments.
> >
> >After the mess that was the run up to 2.0 we all decided to add some more process to try to better manage things.  So
> >far, that has been working in that develop has pretty consistently been in a good state which could generally be
> >released at any moment.  This is a good thing and we should all stop and gives ourselves a little pat on the back about
> >this.
> >
> >Ben is right that Stan needs more users and more developers.  To get more users we need to add more features and make
> >the ones that are there better.  To do that, we need more developers.  (Or more hours in a day...)  Lets be clear about
> >this, Stan as it stands right now is a great tool and it's great that it can be useful to a lot of people but it is NOT
> >a perfect finished product and moving to a development model which is predicated on minimizing change is a bad idea.
> >  Stan needs more work.
> >
> >The problem with the new process is that it is greatly slowing this work.  I'm not just talking about big features and
> >changes but even small simple things.  flexible_adaptation took a month and a half for anyone to so much as comment on.
> >  Other pull requests which provide clear improvements and are unit-tested but may not reach some nirvana-like ideal of
> >unit testing are held in an indefinite limbo (e.g., the LDLT fixes and unit tests).  Yet others which address clearly
> >defined issued have been left with absolutely zero feedback after a month and a half (e.g., readding distance
> >functions).  It feels like the threshold for pull requests to be merged has become "is the feature perfect?" and unless
> >the answer is a clear yes, it doesn't get merged.  That would be fine for a very mature project but Stan is not that.
> >
> >We have maybe a half dozen people contributing to the main Stan project right now and the current process is bogging
> >things down.  If simple pull requests can't be at least *commented on* in a reasonable period of time (a day or two?)
> >something is broken and we're not going to be attracting any more developers.  And, to be blunt, we may start loosing
> >some.  For me right now Stan is not a part of any of my main projects.  I do it mostly in my spare time because I
> >believe the project is important.  For the few side projects where I do use Stan, I've now taken to maintaining a
> >separate branch and my motivation to keep pushing to try to get things merged is dropping with my free time.  I'm not
> >trying to sound petulant here but this is the reality, we're all busy people and we put our efforts where they can be
> >useful.  Unmerged, uncommented pull requests are the opposite of useful.
> >
> >Anyway, hope everyone had a Happy Thanksgiving and stuffed themselves with a suitable amount of tasty food! :)
> >
> >Cheers,
> >Marcus
> >
> >
> >
> >On Fri, Nov 29, 2013 at 11:08 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu <mailto:gel...@stat.columbia.edu>> wrote:
> >
> >
> >    On Nov 29, 2013, at 4:56 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> >>
> >>      * I think the approach Stan has taken to choosing defaults is wrong. It shouldn't be what settings work best for
> >>        most people most of the time. The defaults should be chosen to avoid disastrous behavior as much as possible.
> >>        A small percentage of users can tweak the settings to make it go faster for particular special cases.
> >    Good point, especially if the latter point is clear in the documentation.  At the same time, _if_ an alternative
> >    setting works better in most of the Bugs examples, and we happen to know this, we might as well let people know it.
> >
> >>      * Stan still needs more users and more developers. But I don't think there are many instances where we have
> >>        convinced someone to use Stan over BUGS because the effective sample size per time is larger with Stan. Much
> >>        more often, they have a model that is infeasible in BUGS that turns out to be feasible with Stan. Or
> >>        conversely, they can't switch even though they want to because they heavily use some distribution /
> >>        parameterization that is available for some variant of BUGS but is not in Stan yet.
> >    Interesting point.  Certainly one of my motivations for Stan was because I couldn't fit hierarchical matrix models
> >    in Bugs at all.  And, perhaps even more relevantly, Bugs was a black box.  I never had any idea what Bugs was doing,
> >    or what was happening when it wasn't converging, etc.  It was important for me for Stan to be a program we could get
> >    inside and play with if there was convergence problems.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] factoring RStan, PyStan, etc.
messages.body_plain:
I'm very much in favor of factoring out common code from RStan, PyStan, and
CmdStan. I feel like a few judicious #ifdef's might lighten the load on
everyone.

I'll provide one example:

rstan/rstan/inst/include/rstan/mcmc_output.hpp

and

pystan/mcmc_output.hpp

differ only on 10 lines (out of ~200).

Best,

Allen

On 11/30, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The context of this is that we were discussing adding structured
> mass matrices and I pointed out that for every change to
> command-line Stan, there needs to be a corresponding reimplementation
> in RStan and PyStan.
>
> On 11/30/13, 12:00 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> >Shouldn't the interfaces be factored from these details?
>
> Yes.  As things stand now, anything in stan/gm/command.hpp
> needs to be reimplemented in RStan and PyStan.  So any
> factorization of the code that will minimize the amount of
> code that's directly implemented in the command-line code
> would be a big help.
>
> Also, anything with std::cout, std::cin, or std::cerr
> hardcoded needs to be rewritten for RStan and PyStan.
>
> Another option I've been considering is that we just have
> RStan and PyStan call the command function in Stan directly.
> There are two ways this could work:
>
> Option 1.  RStan and PyStan would:
>
>   * write data and inits to a file,
>   * convert config for the call into the appropriate format,
>   * call a new process to run models that writes output into files, and
>   * read the output back in.
>
> This is what I did originally in the prototype, and then for
> reasons that are now hazy to me, we switched gears to do a deeper
> in-memory integration.  In retrospect, I think this was a mistake.
>
> Option 2:  RStan and PyStan would call the command directly,
> configuring it with the appropriate input, output and error
> streams.  If we do this, we'd need to be much more careful about
> clean resource release (files and memory for now), because
> R and Python are persistent processes, so it's very bad form
> for a function they call to leak resources.
>
> Option 2 is what we were aiming for with RStan, but work on
> the command-line version of Stan has never complied.  One of the
> issues I remember is that holding onto C++ structures and making
> them persistent, which isn't easy in R through Rcpp.  That's
> why the equivalent of the command-line bin/print is also completely
> independently coded in RStan (or at least I think it is).
>
> - Bob
>

I once did a project to optimise the optimisers - I optimised the tuning parameters for genetic algorithms, including weighting and parameters of different operators, including conventional crossover and mutation, plus particle swarm and DE. I guess we could continue the discussion talking about what excites those in academia and enhances their careers and gets papers published, v. what is really important for practitioners. I don't think a post doc would get very excited about spending a year doing testing of existing algorithms, although it requires somebody of post doc capability and experience.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] factoring RStan, PyStan, etc.
messages.body_plain:
Rather than ifdefs, I'd prefer to have reusable base classes or
richer arguments in order to use the language itself rather than
the preprocessor.  It's more modular that way and hence makes
testing from within the language a lot easier, for a start.

For example, we have some things hardcoded for files or for std::cout
that should really be abstracted to deal directly with streams.

Michael's introduction of the mcmc_writer abstraction was intended
as a step in this direction, but it looks like we have further to go.

What I really think we need to do is abstract out the reusable bits
of command.hpp so they can be reused in R/Python/etc. --- that is, if
we don't go the route of just wrapping the command-line version of Stan
in the way that R2WinBUGS and R2jags do.

As far as I/O classes go, there's rarely a reason to make decisions statically
using template parameters or ifdefs as opposed to having more runtime
arguments.

- Bob

On 12/1/13, 9:15 AM, Allen Riddell wrote:
> Hi,
>
> I'll just cast a vote in favor of stability and gradually widening the
> performance gap between JAGS/BUGS.

Thanks for responding.

> Whence my vote for stability? Python does not have JAGS or BUGS so Stan occupies
> a very different position in the statistical computing ecosystem than it does in
> R.

Have you looked at Python packages like emcee, PyMC, PyMCMC, or Theano?
There may not be a BUGS/JAGS wrapper, but there are lots of alternatives,
none of which I've ever tried.  They all seem to be domain specific
EMBEDDED languages, unlike Stan/BUGS/JAGS, which are domain-specific
languages, but not embedded in a particular programming language.

http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domain-specific_language#Usage_patterns

> One serious suggestion: what about a long-term support release cycle like Ubuntu
> that permits rapid development and experimentation in the meantime. For those
> who aren't familiar with this: Ubuntu (Linux) has a very stable release every
> two years that they pledge to support/fix bugs for. Between the LTS releases
> they have other more experimental releases for which they do not pledge the same
> kind of vigilance. This seems to work very well. It's actually a very nice
> contract between developers and users. Users know that they are getting
> something that might have bugs if they don't take the LTS release.

I'd like to hear more about how this works in terms of moving
toward the next stable release.  Does everyone just fork in
the meantime and come back together?  If not, how else are
the changes in the intermediate releases kept compatible with
each other?

If we only had a single stable release, I wouldn't be so
worried.  As is, we've tangled up bug fixes and new features.
Ben may be able to help us on Git process here, which Daniel
and I keep seeming to mess up.

I think the big problem is that nobody has time to do the kind
of support that we need.  For example, I don't think Ben has
the time to be in charge of our Git process, so we rely on
asking his advice from time to time (usually only after we've
dug ourselves into a hole).  Ben, please correct me if I'm wrong --- I'd
be very happy for you to take over on managing the Git side of things!

> Minor point:
>
> - Echoing Jiqiang, I don't want to support Windows on PyStan until/unless
>    a Windows developer joins the PyStan team. I'd like to make this position
>    explicit.

I wish we could do the same for all of Stan!  Windows has caused
us no end of headaches because of its lame C++ tool chain.  Ironically,
for more than a decade, the only way to run BUGS was on Windows!

I don't think we can ignore Windows for R.  Or could we?

My impression is that most of the R community are Windows users.  And to
make matters worse, the RStudio wrapper around R is gaining popularity, which
adds another layer of config complication and indirection.  We have the same
issue with Rcpp, because none of the Rcpp devs have Windows machines (or at
least none did when I unsubsscribed to their list after asking a few questions).

- Bob

On 12/1/13, 5:35 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:

>> The only thing I was thinking about doing was using
>> template instantiations as we do for the grammars
>> so these become one-time speed costs at the expense of
>> using much more memory.  This is just the template lib
>> version of breaking a lib into .cpp and .hpp file.
>
> Is it not possible to do the same thing with the rest of Stan the library? Like instantiate one dynamically resizeable
> Cholesky object with our scalar types?

It's pretty straightforward.  Especially for Cholesky,
which only has two instantiations until we add RHMC,
namely Matrix<double> and Matrix<var>.

The problem is that we have a lot of functions and many of
them are far more polymorphic than the Cholesky decomposition.

The worst case is for now is the Student-t density function,
which has four arguments,  each of which can be instantiated by

    double, var,
    vector<double>, vector<var>,
    row-vector<double>, row-vector<var>,
    vector<var>, vector<double>, for a total of 8^4 (4096) instantiations.

I don't think that will be feasible in terms of compilation time
or object code size.

With the header-based approach we take now, only the instances that
are used in a particular model get instantiated and compiled, though
it has to be done on a model-per-model basis.

- Bob

messages.subject: precompiling RStan vs. process dependency
messages.body_plain:
The only thing we can precompile for RStan is stanc and the
posterior analysis tools (equivalent of bin/print in
the command-line Stan).  We could already precompile these if we wanted
to.  Then we'd still need to be able to compile models dynamically,
which means we need the entire tool chain, including Rcpp and
a recent enough C++ compiler.  And we'd still have the same issue
with R's global config of compiler options to contend with.

So I still don't think being distributed on CRAN is
going to make it much easier for users to get the whole system
working.  It will make the initial install easier and make us
easier to find.  Maybe it will give us more credibility with R users.

Here's the alternative I'm currently thinking is best:

Refactor RStan so that it calls Stan command-line in
a separate process (or processes).  This is the way that R2WinBUGS and
R2jags work.  This has a number of pleasant properties:

   * make it trivial to update RStan for new versions of Stan

   * completely eliminate the possiblity of Stan crashing R or
     leaking resources like memory or file handles in R

   * make it trivial to get onto CRAN

   * move the responsibility for supporting Windows, RStudio, etc.,
     off of the RStan maintainers and put it in a single place that
     is going to be maintained anyway

   * move the responsibility for the majority of doc off of
     Rstan  --- RStan will only need to point to the Stan command-line
     doc for configuring the actual samplers

   * remove the Rcpp dependency from RStan

I think this is the way we have to go longer term to reduce the number
of dependencies in the project and make it maintainable going forward.
It will require more disk-based I/O:

   * RStan will need to write data to file (already implemented with RStan's dump)

   * RStan will need to read Stan's CSV output (also already implemented)

I now realize that neither of these are really bottlenecks for RStan.

It will also require:

   * RStan will need to know where Stan is installed

   * RStan users will need to install Stan

I actually think the latter won't be much harder than getting RStan
installed --- we can still let them install Ripley's toolchain for
Windows, use Xcode for the Mac, and let Linux users have whatever
version of makefile and clang++ or g++ they want as long as it's
recent enough.

- Bob

R2jags and R2WinBUGS do, which is require the R lib to be configured
with the location of JAGS or BUGS.

> that difficult to do.

Jiqiang reported that he didn't want to deal with
Windows.  Allen said the same thing w.r.t. PyStan.
RStudio's caused some issues that would go away.
And installing Rcpp has been the major pain, though
we're left with a large part of that pain in getting the
toolchain installed.

I think porting the command as it stands is pretty challenging.
Jiqiang's done a great job of it, but it's still work and it's
still error prone and it still means every time we change Stan's command
line, we have to change RStan and PyStan.  A process-based approach reduces
dependencies.  It means we only have to update RStan when the
output of Stan command-line changes formats, which we don't anticipate
happening as frequently as the sampler and its config through args gets
updated.

Porting would be easier if we make the Stan samplers and optimizers
more modular and less tied into the command line.

> Stan and it wouldn't be possible with array (std::vector) types, because

We have two extra copies of the data then because R copies the data by default before passing it to an external library. One can be turned off by specifying DUP = FALSE, which is safe when the external library does not modify the data (in R's workspace). But if Stan is making another copy anyway, then there is not much of an advantage to the in-memory approach.

> > In any event, if we could just have users do
> > install.packages("rstan") and have it prompt to install Rtools if necessary, that would minimize the problems.
>
> Yes, that would be great.  That's still just stanc and libstan, though.
> And I'm not sure how much libstan is even saving us in compile time
> for models vs. a header-only approach.

We have not had many instances on stan-users where someone had a valid model that couldn't be compiled on their machine. We have had parser bugs that were producing flawed C++ and a lot of problems building stanc. So, if we could get CRAN to provide binary installation of stanc, we would be 90% of the way there (particularly since rstan could check for the existence of a C++ compiler and offer to download / install one if it is not found).

> We could distribute Windows binaries of it ourselves.  In
> fact, we probably should given the problems people have been
> having getting it to build given Windows' poor tool chain.

I wouldn't want anyone to trust us with binaries that we generate / sign ourselves. People should barely be trusting the binaries they get from CRAN.

> > We just
> > have to get the binary package to build on the CRAN servers.
>
> No idea what that entails.  Making the model compiles go faster
> by precompiling things is probably in direct opposition to getting
> CRAN to build our packages for us.

It's documented pretty extensively

http://cran.r-project.org/doc/manuals/r-release/R-exts.html

but the short version is that rstan was rejected the first time for including many MB of Boost.

So, we could say that Boost is a SystemRequirement in rstan's DESCRIPTION file, in which case it would probably be fine for rstan to bundle src/stan/ and maybe lib/eigen_*. But I don't think we could get away with saying that a specific version of Boost is a SystemRequirement because CRAN won't promise to install that version (it probably has 1.48 or 1.49 or something installed).

Or we could say that Stan is a SystemRequirement, in which case it would have whatever version of Boost and Eigen that we have under lib. And CRAN does install open-source libraries on the CRAN servers that R packages access. But I don't think they would be happy to update CRAN's copy of Stan very often since it requires doing so on 3 platforms by a human who disagrees with this non-UNIX approach to packaging and distributing software anyway.

Or we can say that the BH R package is a Depends of rstan. In that case, rstan would include Stan (sans most of boost but maybe with Eigen and a few parts of Boost) and builds stanc, libstan, etc. This is what I think would be best because we could update rstan once a month if we wanted to and no human associated with CRAN has to do much. That would require that Stan build with the version of Boost in BH plus whatever parts of Boost that rstan includes but I don't think that is very daunting (I did it a few weeks ago).

> > I can see the value in having the rstan package just make system calls, but that is a separate issue from what to do
> > about CRAN or whether rstan should include Stan.
>
> It won't help us get on CRAN if there isn't any C++ code
> in RStan?   I thought that'd make it trivial, but admit I
> know squat about CRAN or R package build and distribution.

There are tons of R packages that use C++ (although nowdays most do so via Rcpp). Our problems with CRAN before weren't even technical. But under the non-CRAN approach I think you prefer, we have to get all the (mostly Windows) users to build stanc and libstan locally and then install our rstan package from GitHub and get it talking to the local installation of Stan. And I am skeptical that will be much of a net gain from where we are now. It could be a net loss. But I don't think having rstan on CRAN would help much if it required users and CRAN to have a local installation of Stan. Conversely, I think it would be worth almost any cost if we could get binary installations of rstan from CRAN that didn't require a local installation of Stan.

Ben

I think this latter statement is where we fundamentally disagree.

I'd say that avoiding dependencies is worth almost any cost.
We're going to have the same issues with Python, Debian and other
Linux distros, Stata, etc., and I have a very strong preference for
minimizing the dependencies in both the code and between Stan
and its interfaces over making it slightly easier for users to install.
If we keep the interfaces abstracted from the executables of Stan,
all of these dependencies goes away.

This is exactly the kind of issue we have no process in place to
resolve.  Reasonable people can disagree about priorities.

Does anyone else have any opinions?  This is a decision that will impact
what we can do in the Stan C++ API, as well as in the CmdStan, RStan
and PyStan interfaces, assuming we want RStan to be able to keep up with
CmdStan.

And if so, then it would be a collective responsibility for us to deal with that person rather than something that falls more heavily on Mav and me. I guess I just feel that an installation problem is an installation problem, so if there is one I will probably reply on stan-users unless it is a Mac thing that I don't know anything about. Yes, we have those issues, but Debian in particular will refuse as a matter of policy to embed Boost or Eigen with Stan for security reasons primarily. (and I'm pretty sure every Linux distro has that policy). You are only allowed to use one of the versions of Boost that is available in a particular repository. At the moment, Debian is trying to get Boost 1.54 into the next stable version of Debian which is likely a year or more away and the latest stable version of Debian has Boost 1.49. So, dealing with multiple versions of Boost or Eigen or refraining from updating Boost in Stan is inevitable if Stan (or PyStan) is ever going to be packages for Linux distros. But it is not a huge deal. Someone discovers that Stan doesn't work with some version of Boost on ARM or MIPS or whatever and they usually send you a patch to fix it.

> This is exactly the kind of issue we have no process in place to
> resolve.  Reasonable people can disagree about priorities.

I agree we are making predictions about the future states of the world. But I am influenced a lot by the experience of Sage, which is an open-source alternative to Mathematica and other closed-source math software, and they bundle all of their (dozens of) dependencies into a 340+ MB tarball with particular (and sometimes patched) versions:

http://www.sagemath.org/packages/standard/

And that makes it easier to write code. But they get a ton of emails from users that can't build it successfully on their machine and ask why they need to build such and such when they already have that installed. And someone spent a lot of time getting everything packaged for Debian experimental but it eventually got kicked out of Debian. Then they got a GSOC student to refactor everything so Sage could utilize system dependencies and thus be easier for Linux distros to package, but then Sage wouldn't accept the patches. Basically, it has been a giant mess and for most of the Mathematica users that they are trying to lure away, I think it would have been much easier if they had sought to do binary installation of the dependencies from the outset.

Ben

[Redirected to -dev]

Profiling the code showed that it was spending most of the time in the
unlist method called by sapply in the first line of
            fun1 <- function(par) {
              sss <- sapply(tidx[[par]], get_kept_samples2, object@sim)
              if (is.list(sss))  sss <- do.call(c, sss)
              dim(sss) <- c(sum(n_kept), object@sim$dims_oi[[par]])
              dimnames(sss) <- list(iterations = NULL)
              sss
            }
that is part of  the extract method for stanfit.  This function is
called only if permute is true.

Why that's so slow I don't know.  Using lapply instead of sapply runs
fast for that line, but triggers the do.call(c, sss) on the next line,
which is about as slow as the original.  However,
            fun1 <- function(par) {
              sss <- lapply(tidx[[par]], rstan:::get_kept_samples2, object@sim)
              if (is.list(sss))  sss <- do.call(cbind, sss)
              dim(sss) <- c(sum(n_kept), object@sim$dims_oi[[par]])
              dimnames(sss) <- list(iterations = NULL)
              sss
            }

Runs much faster (since I defined the test function outside of the
package scope I needed to explicitly qualify calls to internal package
functions).

e1 is the original extract; e2 is the new version.
> system.time(t1 <- e1(myfit))
    user  system elapsed
  11.420   0.004  11.463
 > system.time(t2 <- e2(myfit))
    user  system elapsed
   0.396   0.008   0.405
!> identical(t1, t2)
 [1] TRUE

I think the lines
              if (is.list(sss))  sss <- do.call(cbind, sss)
              dim(sss) <- c(sum(n_kept), object@sim$dims_oi[[par]])
could be converted to
		do.call(cbind, sss)
but perhaps I'm missing some subtlety.  As I said, they look as if they
might be a holdover from an earlier implementation.

Ross

The sense in which unlist is called by sapply may not be obvious (it
wasn't to me)--it has nothing to do with the get_kept_samples2 function.
Rather, sapply is
> sapply
 function (X, FUN, ..., simplify = TRUE, USE.NAMES = TRUE)
 {
     FUN <- match.fun(FUN)
     answer <- lapply(X = X, FUN = FUN, ...)
     if (USE.NAMES && is.character(X) && is.null(names(answer)))
         names(answer) <- X
     if (!identical(simplify, FALSE) && length(answer))
         simplify2array(answer, higher = (simplify == "array"))
     else answer
 }
and simplify2array ultimately calls unlist.

Here's a sample call stack from Rprof:

(outermost call on the right, apparently, and "FUN" is the function fun1 in the source).

Allen:  You're driving the PyStan bus, so it's
really up to you at this point!

You could pass a socket address for reading to Stan rather
than a file name.  I'm not sure what the support is in C++
or Boost for this --- if it's as easy as in Java, it shouldn't
be a problem to generalize our file arguments to sockets.
And ideally, we could even do HTTP to read web-served files;
that's also trivial in Java, but I have no experience doing it in C++.

- Bob

> * it need do the boundary check, which makes it inefficient
> * the thinning makes the index for iteration ambiguous

More generally, it's unclear exactly what interface would be of general
interest.  I originally was thinking

stanfit[i, j, k] where i is chain, j is step and k
is coefficient.

As you point out, one might want j to be before or after thinning.
k could be an index (in the total index sense used internally), a string
like the values of pars, or booleans.  The total index seems an
unfriendly interface, though perhaps if some of the related functions
were exposed it would make sense.

One might want to overlook the chains and use
stanfit[n, k]  where n is the n'th sample (combining all chains), and k
indexes a parameter.

It might need some caching (e.g., of the total indices for a named
parameter) to be effficient.  I'm not sure it needs bounds checking; I
think it will just throw an error if one attempts an out of bounds
access.

There are also several choices about what gets returned.

All of which is  to agree that the time is not ripe for implementing [].
Now that extract is faster I feel less need to work around it.

Ross

Re: [stan-dev] triangle model
messages.body_plain:
:-)  This is exactly what I did when running this the first
time.  It's a good warning about how means and variances can
look pretty good even though the outer quantiles look very
bad.

I believe this is an example where targeting a higher
acceptance probability will help you get further into
the tails and reduce the downward bias in variance estimate
you get from not going into the tails.

So you might want to try it with a higher accept
target and see what happens to the variance and quantile estimates.

We really need to start the Stan column on your blog!

- Bob

> I'm confused.  Why is there blur in the relation between y and lp__?  Shouldn't the relation be deterministic?

It is just a two-dimensional kernel density plot. So,

log(1 - abs(y))

varies with y but also because lp__ is defined with respect to the unconstrained space instead of the (-1,1) interval on which y is supported.

Basically, the color intensity just shows that there is a big difference in lp__ at the mode relative to the tails.

Ben

triangle <- stan_demo(“triangle”, iter = 100000, control = list(adapt_delta = 0.8))

> This is not a big deal, but . . . my sense is that in R, numbers are real numbers ("double") unless otherwise stated.

You're right --- R doc doesn't state types of arguments
either way.  So if you see something like rnorm(), you see:

   x, q
   vector of quantiles.

   p
   vector of probabilities.

   n
   number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.

Yet another reason I find all the R doc so opaque.  You never write
doc for a real programming language without specifying the type of
the arguments.  So I guess "number of" and the variable name "n"
is supposed to clue you in.

> Just for example, if you look at help(par) for graphical parameters, there are various numeric options, and they are not identified as "numeric" or "double" or anything like that, they're simply stated as "The figure region dimensions, (width, height), in inches" or whatever.

help(par) is some of the most confusing doc I've ever read!
But you're right that they don't specify types.

> So in stan(), we could have a parameter that is "The target acceptance rate (must be between 0 and 1, default is 0.8)" or whatever.

Whatever you guys think is best for RStan.

My inclinations are competing with each other:

   -- be explicit about all argument types
   -- be idiomatic and stick to the language conventions

- Bob

> Only that Stan itself copies the data in its model constructor.
> Nothing you can do about that from the outside.  We could potentially
> rewrite it so that if the memory were local coming from R, we could
> share the memory in Eigen using Map.  It'd be a pretty big change to
> Stan and it wouldn't be possible with array (std::vector) types, because
> they don't have constructors that don't copy the data (at least as far

FYI: I got the following to work in a couple of minutes, which uses memory-mapped files

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/doc/html/interprocess/sharedmemorybetweenprocesses.html#interprocess.sharedmemorybetweenprocesses.mapped_file
http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory-mapped_file

that ostensibly allow the application to work with files on disk that are bigger than the available RAM and the OS manages what parts of the file it needs at a particular time.

#include <boost/interprocess/file_mapping.hpp>
#include <boost/interprocess/mapped_region.hpp>
#include <Eigen/Dense>
#include <iostream>

int main() {
  using namespace boost::interprocess;

  file_mapping m_file("test.bin", read_only);

  const std::size_t FileSize = 10000;      // too big but works
  mapped_region region(m_file, read_only);

  double *mem = static_cast<double*>(region.get_address());
  Eigen::Map<Eigen::MatrixXd> m(mem, 10, 3);

  std::cout << m << std::endl;

  return 0;
}

>     You're right --- R doc doesn't state types of arguments
>     either way.  So if you see something like rnorm(), you see:
>
>         x, q
>         vector of quantiles.
>
>         p
>         vector of probabilities.
>
>         n
>         number of observations. If length(n) > 1, the length is taken to be the number required.
>
>     Yet another reason I find all the R doc so opaque.  You never write
>     doc for a real programming language without specifying the type of
>     the arguments.  So I guess "number of" and the variable name "n"
>     is supposed to clue you in.
>
>
> Well, in fairness to R, as long as you pass it a number, it works. And you get an error message otherwise

This is exactly what I don't like about R!

It will automatically coerce non-integers to integers with no
warnings:

   > rnorm(n = 2.9)
   [1] -0.7523264 -0.8288448

How often is this going to be intentional vs. a programming error?

And it's not just R.  C++ has the same behavior.  For instance, in:

   int main() {
     double xd = 2.7;
     int x = xd;
     int y = 2.1;
     std::cout << x << ", " << y << std::endl;
   }

there's only a warning for the literal conversion:

   ~/temp2$ clang++ bar.cpp
   bar.cpp:6:11: warning: implicit conversion from 'double' to 'int' changes value from 2.1 to 2 [-Wliteral-conversion]
     int y = 2.1;
         ~   ^~~
   1 warning generated.

   ~/temp2$ ./a.out
   2, 2

Stan, on the other hand, was designed to work like Java, where you
get an error if you try to assign a real value to an integer value
or pass a real value into a function expecting an integer.

> I think once Mike's flexibile adaptation branch is merged, then we will have to face the question of whether to rewrite
> RStan to do system calls, in which case it won't matter much because all the arguments will be dumped into a character
> string.

There will still be the issue of how much of the CmdStan doc to
copy over into the stan() doc for RStan.  None of it's one viable
option, which has the advantage of always being consistent and requiring
no work to maintain.

> But in the meantime, I don't think we have to be explicit about the types because they are internally coerced to
> the correct type before calling the compiled function.

Whatever you guys think is best for RStan is OK with me.

- Bob

I started out being very worried about both memory consumption and
I/O issues from data, but I now realize that Stan isn't fast enough to
deal with data sets that would give memory problems and that the I/O
time is dominated by sampling time.  The auto-diff will kill us before lack
of memory sharing will.

Nifty.  I didn't even know Boost had it.  Usually you use
memory mapping for non-random access to files.

It'll be significantly slower (many orders of magnitude)
than in memory for random access, more so if the machine
has spinny disks instead of solid state.

But if you have multiple processes hitting the same memory-mapped
file, you get disk-head contention (again, the problem's there
but less so with SSDs because seek times are several orders of
magnitude faster) --- with spinny disk it takes multiple milliseconds
(more than 5 last time I checked) for the first random access byte from a
file system.

If the data can be pipelined, it can be relatively efficient,
but then so is non-memory mapped I/O.

There's a great package called Vowpal Wabbit (an Elmer Fudd pronouncing
Monty Python referring to Lewis Carroll -- and you thought Andrew's
names were obscure), which does stochastic gradient desecent on huge
files by streaming data from file as needed.  We are going to have to
start thinking about these issues when our stochastic VB gets off
the ground.  Matt's stochastic variational implementation of LSA got
rolled into Vowpal Wabbit, but I think VW is mostly used for linear/logistic
regression and CRF/MRF type problems.  VW also does really cool things
with dimensionality reduction using hash-based feature encodings.  Not
exactly the way social scientists want to roll!

- Bob

> parallel. I'm sure there would still be performance tradeoffs, but I doubt many Stan models are doing much random access

If we want to fit a simple GLM with a lot of data, the auto-diff memory size will
be small relative to the data size.  Then, if the predictors are kept memory
local (e.g., array of Eigen vectors, or columns of an Eigen matrix), then
something like this might make sense.  For more complex models, auto-diff memory
requirements will be the main bottleneck.

I'm guessing it would still be faster to just run the chains one at a time
rather than in parallel with memory mapping to disk I/O.

- Bob

These questions are mostly for Micheal. I've asked before, but it got buried in other discussion.

In src/stan/gm/command.hpp, when a sampler is called and we start warmup, under most samplers we call:
   init_adapt<sampler>(sampler_ptr, adapt)  (lines 835-875)

This calls:
   s->init_stepsize() (line 231)

When we start init_stepsize(), the sampler's position elements are always initialized with 0.

**** Questions ***
Is this the intended behavior?
Should we be adapting an initial stepsize starting from the initialization? (we've already drawn the initial values or loaded the file by this point)
Or should we be starting from a different starting point?
Or... does it not matter, which is why it's starting at 0?

Daniel

messages.subject: stepsizes
messages.body_plain:
This is pretty much a question for Mike:

I was just wondering if it would make sense to adapt to multiple step sizes.  The simplest approach would be to do a separate adaptation for each chain, then suppose they came up with step sizes a,b,c,d.  Then in the HMC, we could rotate thru these 4 values for each chain.  The advantage would be that if different step sizes are better for different parts of the space, we'd get multiple chances to get a good value.  And a really crappy value would not kill a chain, as it would only be used 1/4 of the time (for simplicity I'm assuming 4 chains here).

We could use the same idea for adapting mass matrices.  We'd have multiple mass matrices (or multiple scaling vectors, if we're just adapting on the diagonals).

Yes, I realize that RMHMC is much more sophisticated, but in the context of static Nuts, what do you think?

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
messages.body_plain:
We currently have an option for jittering step size.

Communication across chains will require:

   * inter-process communication and synchronization to run
     in parallel

   * running just warmup in sequence, saving results, then
     restarting in sequence

Many of the things we'd have to do to the code to support
these two approaches would be shared.  But then it brings
up how fine-grained we want inter-chain communication to be.
This is just one synch point, which is relatively easy compared
to more frequent and asynchronous inter-chain communication.

Another thought is that if we have the intention of covering
a space that might have varying geometry, we may want to design
the parallel warmup to try to do some kind of reasonable cover.
Right now, we're only trying to learn a single global mass matrix,
which as we know is inappropriate for hierarchical models like
the funnel.

- Bob

On 12/6/13, 11:17 AM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> This is pretty much a question for Mike:
>
> I was just wondering if it would make sense to adapt to multiple step sizes.  The simplest approach would be to do a separate adaptation for each chain, then suppose they came up with step sizes a,b,c,d.  Then in the HMC, we could rotate thru these 4 values for each chain.  The advantage would be that if different step sizes are better for different parts of the space, we'd get multiple chances to get a good value.  And a really crappy value would not kill a chain, as it would only be used 1/4 of the time (for simplicity I'm assuming 4 chains here).
>
> We could use the same idea for adapting mass matrices.  We'd have multiple mass matrices (or multiple scaling vectors, if we're just adapting on the diagonals).
>
> Yes, I realize that RMHMC is much more sophisticated, but in the context of static Nuts, what do you think?
>
> A
>
>

messages.body_plain:
So this kind of strategy would really be appropriate for posteriors with multiple modes, each with different curvature.
The big issues we're seeing are with models where the curvature changes continuously, and consequently almost
all of the chains will really average over the curvature instead of adapt to just a local region.  In other words,  trying
to get multiple chains with different step sizes will be difficult.

Then there's the issue of varying the step size.  Without being able to select the step size based on the local curvature
you'll get significant inefficiencies.

I think the big potential gain with interchain communication is in learning the global curvature quickly (i.e. not limited
by large autocorrelation early in a single chain) which would speed up warmup.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stepsizes
messages.body_plain:
Yes, it's a failure of adaptation, but if we run 4 chains and each gives a different mass matrix, and 3 are good and 1 is bad, then rotating through the 4 will give us an efficiency of 3/4, which is far better than having 3 chains humming fine and 1 chain stuck in disaster mode.

We could even move form a 2-stage to a 4-stage process.  Right now, stage 1 is adaptation and stage 2 is running the chains.  One problem with the current system is that stage 1 can go very slowly, another problem is that if we get a shitty mass matrix in stage 1, we're fucked in stage 2.  My above suggestion should fix the problem in stage 2, but we'd still be going slow in stage 1.

The new plan could be:  stage -1 is initial adaptation giving initial mass matrices.  Stage 0 is running by rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage -1.  Then Stage 1 is adaptation again.  And Stage 2 is the production runs, with each chain rotating thru the 4 mass matrices obtained in stage 1.  The point of Stages -1 and 0 in this new version is to more effectively move us away from bad places so we're less likely to get stuck in stage 1.

messages.body_plain:
> In any case, though, even with a flexible adaptation, I'd think that in a non-Riemannian setting, a typical distribution would work better with an ensemble of mass matrices rather than a single mass matrix.  And, with an ensemble, rotating through seems like a pretty robust way to get the benefits.

I am not as confident in the ultimate utility as you are.  The problem is how well can you actually learn the optimal distribution and what is the variance of that distribution?  Even if you can learn it correctly you'll introduce a cost proportionally to the standard deviation in the best case -- in the case of hierarchical models where the distribution would be skewed the cost would be even worse.

Again, the only circumstance I can think of where such a strategy would work is when the optimal distribution is multimodal and in that case we have bigger issues to deal with.

The real issue here isn't that the target distribution has multiple scales and the adaptation of each chain is learning a unique scale but rather that the adaptation in one of the chains screws up and converges to a poor value that doesn't represent any of the correct scales.

messages.subject: Moving From std::vector to Eigen::Vector
messages.body_plain:
There are two ways to proceed:

Change the samplers and autodiff to use Eigen::Vector but leave the internal model storage as std::vector

or

Convert everything to Eigen::Vector

Given how the model is abstracted through the autodiff functors both should be equally feasible.  Does anyone have any preferences?

On 12/6/13, 7:09 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> There are two ways to proceed:
>
> Change the samplers and autodiff to use Eigen::Vector but leave the internal model storage as std::vector

Do you mean the signature of the log probability method
in a model class?

Changing it will require changing the transform methods from constrained
to unconstrained and back.

This will in turn affect RStan and PyStan, though it
should be an easy change.

> Convert everything to Eigen::Vector
>
> Given how the model is abstracted through the autodiff functors both should be equally feasible.  Does anyone have any preferences?

We need Eigen::Matrix in order to return results like Jacobians
efficiently.  So the autodiff functors pretty much have to be
done in terms of Eigen outputs.

I think the functional passed to the autodiff functors should
operate on the same type of parameter sequence as is used for
the model's log probability function.

- Bob

P.S.  Extra credit for removing the detritus from assuming there might
       eventually be integer parameters --- eve if we do add them some day,
       they may not be like what are stubbed out.

messages.subject: Re: stepsizes
messages.body_plain:
How do you detect disaster in a chain?

During burn-in, I allow a 'reset', which re-estimates a starting step size. I reapply find_reasonable_epsilon, and re-estimate a mass matrix.

I do this when alpha/nalpha < 1.0e-10 and depth >= maxDepth

This was purely from experience when the step size collapsed, and it seemed to do it when those conditions were observed.

Resets are common in optimisation algorithms, when certain conditions are observed.

Because my function/derivative evaluation is complex and I can multi thread at that level, I do not multi thread at the chain level. So I can easily communicate between chains. This is needed anyway when I use e.g. DREAM samplers. Rolling DREAM and other samplers into the mix of course also avoids any one chain becoming stuck. If you multi thread at the chain level (which I can understand is your preferred approach), then communicating becomes difficult, especially if the elapsed time per sample varies a lot - which it will do if each chain uses NUTS, and even more so if different chains use different samplers.

My current approach is to have a common stepsize etc. across all chains, so every chain is used as input into a common adaptor. This will also help avoid sticking.

Maybe there is some conflict between the best multi threaded implementation architecture, and the best single threaded algorithm? Which is the cart, which is the horse? If communication is rare, then having a chain waiting until all other chains have reached a 'checkpoint' should not be difficult to implement.

Trying to handle multiple modes which have different optimal step sizes/masss matrices is a whole other issue - and you certainly don't want a chain stuck in a single mode. I mix in DREAM mainly for this reason. Same for models with discrete variables.

I do, of course, jitter the step size. I jitter with a 10% Gaussian distribution, but I did try at one time with a gamma distribution.

It makes me wonder - does your implementation architecture easily allow a chain to rotate (or randomly choose) different samplers? Not just during burn-in? This may be long term a more important issue than the chain sticking problem.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-dev] Re: Moving From std::vector to Eigen::Vector
messages.body_plain:
On 12/6/13, 9:16 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Friday, December 6, 2013 7:09:04 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
>     There are two ways to proceed:
>
>     Change the samplers and autodiff to use Eigen::Vector but leave the internal model storage as std::vector
>
>     or
>
>     Convert everything to Eigen::Vector
>
>     Given how the model is abstracted through the autodiff functors both should be equally feasible.  Does anyone have
>     any preferences?
>
>
> Um, what is the problem that these two proposals are a solution to? Maybe using an Eigen::Map is a third possibility?

The underlying use is now as an Eigen vector and we wind up
either wrapping or copying the std::vector coming in.

I don't think we want Eigen::Map as the input type --- it's just
one of many expression template-like types that Eigen uses.
Ben's pointed us before to Eigen's advice on how to do these
arguments more generally so as to accept references to expression
templates:

   http://eigen.tuxfamily.org/dox/TopicFunctionTakingEigenTypes.html

We could start following this advice, but it may be more trouble
than it's worth in this case.  And it will, of course, introduce
more deeply nested template parameter fiddling at compile time.

> I'm pretty sure I would be in favor of converting everything to Eigen types regardless. It is one thing to say that we
> should limit the number of libraries that we depend on (although I am not totally convinced of that).  But given that
> Stan fundamentally depends on a library such as Eigen (and it would be non-trivial to even swap in another matrix

> library like Armadillo), then we should use Eigen as much as possible because it is awesome.'

Stan's samplers did not in the past fundamentally depend on Eigen.
Michael's refactor of the samplers in 2.0 introduced the dependency.
Adding the dependency makes sense when you start manipulating the
parameter vector as a mathematical vector, as Michael's doing.

Stan's model base class still (v2.0.1) does not depend on Eigen,
so this proposed change would be introducing a dependency.

Of course, all of our generated models depend on everything.  This
is not good, but it'd be a big programming project to trim everything
and would require the code generator to keep track of dependencies on
every function it generates, which means a dependency of the code generator
on every specific function we introduce to ensure its dependencies are included.
Not having this dependency makes it easier to introduce new functions.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I'm pulling this out of the issue discussion and put a discussion
on our Wiki, which I linked from the Wiki home:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Coding-Style-and-Idioms

To summarize:

Here are the types to use for indexes and sizes of std::vector and Eigen::Matrix:

   * size_t for std::vector

   * int for Eigen::Matrix<T,R,C>

   * T::size_type for template params T that can be instantiated
     to either

One could argue we should always use Eigen::Matrix<S,R,C>::size_type for Eigen constructs
just in case we ever decide that we want to change their default indexing from int
to something else. But int should be OK for now because if we change the index type for some
reason, the compiler will let us find instances.

(In 2.0.1, you see both approaches used for Eigen in prob/transform.hpp.)

- Bob

Note that this drops "_factor" from "cholesky_factor".

their usage.

spd is a good convention, but

>    spd_matrix
>    corr_matrix
>    spd_cholesky
>    corr_cholesky

spd_cholesky is not good. The Cholesky factor itself is not spd and the matrix that it is a Cholesky factor of is spd by construction.

> or to:
>
>    matrix_spd
>    matrix_corr
>    cholesky_spd
>    cholesky_corr

I do think it makes more sense for the cholesky_ to come first, since in English we usually say that "L is the Cholesky factor of Sigma" rather than "Sigma's Cholesky factor is L". But by that logic, matrix_spd and matrix_corr sound backwards.

> or be even more fully qualified:
>
>    matrix
>    matrix_spd
>    matrix_spd_unit_diag
>    matrix_cholesky_spd
>    matrix_cholesky_spd_unit_diag

These seem too verbose. And more Stan users are more likely to understand what a corr_matrix is than to know that a matrix_spd_unit_diag is a correlation matrix.

In other words, corr_matrix was always unambiguous, although we need something unambiguous to refer to its Cholesky factor. But cov_matrix was misleading because it was never required to actually be a covariance matrix. So, having spd_matrix subsume cov_matrix is fine, I think.

messages.subject: rethinking PyStan's and RStan's relation to Stan - not!
messages.subject_clean: rethinking PyStan's and RStan's relation to Stan - not!
messages.body_plain:
I've been thinking more about having PyStan and RStan
just call an installed version of Stan.

The plus side is that it gets around this wrestling match
we're having with R's build process.  It means much less
duplicated code.

Looking more deeply at the RStan interface, this is going
to be problematic for implementing many of the model-based
functions that Jiqiang's implemented:

    -- converting unconstrained to constrained parameters

    -- calling log prob from model

    -- calling gradient (or Hessian) from model

None of these would be impossible to do in RStan where
models were compiled into their own executables, but it
would require

    -- adding these functions to the main() in CmdStan

    -- taking the hit to pass them into the main(), either
       by file or socket or whatever

I think the better approach might be to try to abstract
the commands in CmdStan so that they're easier to access in
RStan and PyStan.  As is, I fear there's too much duplication
of code --- everything in the CmdStan's src/stan/gm/command.hpp
needs to be recoded in PyStan or RStan.

- Bob

messages.subject: unfolding 2nd/3rd-order auto-diff
messages.body_plain:
Michael wants to speed up the 2nd and 3rd order auto-diff
types fvar<var> and fvar<fvar<var> > that we need for RHMC.
(We also need fvar<var> for Hessian calcs.)

The only way I see to do that is by unfolding (partially
evaluating) the derivatives that we'd get by brute-force
auto-diff.

I'm going to use exp(x) as an example.  Binary ops go the same
way, but with twice as many input terms.

2nd Order
---------

Here's how exp() looks in agrad/fwd:

   template <typename T>
   inline
   fvar<T> exp(const fvar<T>& x) {
     return fvar<T>(exp(x.val_), x.d_ * exp(x.val_));
   }

This would be better coded without the duplicated exp() application as:

   template <typename T>
   inline
   fvar<T> exp(const fvar<T>& x) {
     T exp_x_v = exp(x.val_);
     return fvar<T>(exp_x_v, x.d_ * exp_x_v);
   }

Instantiating with T=var in the second-order case yields

   inline
   fvar<var> exp(const fvar<var>& x) {
     var exp_x_v = exp(x.val_);
     return fvar<var>(exp_x_v,
                      x.d_ * exp_x_v);
   }

Given that we have good implementations of exp(var) and (var * var),
I don't see how this could be sped up at all.

3rd Order
---------

Instantiating T to fvar<var> in the templated implementation of exp(),
we get:

   inline
   fvar<fvar<var> > exp(const fvar<fvar<var> >& x) {
     return fvar<fvar<var> >(exp(x.val_), x.d_ * exp(x.val_));
   }

The key to going further is to unfold x into its value and tangent
components:

   (a,b) = (x.val_, x.d_)

for which the types of a and b are fvar<var>, so themselves can
be unfolded into value and tangent components:

   a = (c,d) = (x.val_.val_, x.val_.d_)
   b = (e,f) = (x.d_.val_, x.d_.d_)

The types of c, d, e, and f are var.

Then you need to plug in and evaluate, which I find easier to
do in brackets notation:

    exp([(c,d),(e,f)])                   // 3rd order op

    =  [exp(c,d), (e,f) * exp(c,d)]      // 2nd order ops

    =  [( exp(c),                        // 1st order ops
          d * exp(c) ),
        ( e * exp(c),
          e * exp(c) * d + f * exp(c) ) ]

Thus we can write out the specialization to fvar<fvar<var> > as:

   inline
   fvar<fvar<var> > exp(const fvar<fvar<var> >& x) {
     var c = x.val_.val_;
     var d = x.val_.d_;
     var e = x.d_.val_;
     var f = x.d_.d_;
     var exp_c = exp(c);
     var e_times_exp_c = e * exp_c;
     return fvar<fvar<var> >(fvar<var>(exp_c,
                                       d * exp_c),
                             fvar<var>(e_times_exp_c,
                                       e_times_exp_c * d + f * exp_c));
   }

Everything from the template instantiation should get inlined
and essentially produce code equal to the above (I think --- I may
be missing something that'd get calculated twice).  It's hard
to predict compiler behavior, so maybe it'd be better to write
it out explicitly anyway.  I'm not sure if it'd be easier to read by
renaming variables c to vv, d to vd, e to dv, and f to dd.

Also, we don't really need the e and f temps as they don't get reused.

The only speedup I can see helping on top of this is to write
a custom vari extension for:

   foo(u,v,w,x) = u * v + w * x

This would be substantially faster than evaluating the expression in
the last line of (6), which puts three expressions on the expression
tree and requires three virtual calls instead of one.  We only need the
function for var inputs here, so we might as well just implement the
vari specialization directly instead of the function.  No need to expose
this 2D dot-product function in the Stan language itself.

exp() is relatively easy.  But we can work on a few functions at a time
because it's only adding speed, not functionality.

The test should be of all four values (c,d,e,f) and their derivatives
against the explicit template specialization.  But I'm not sure how we
can force the compiler to use the less specialized function for one call and
the more specialized one for another if they're in the same namespace.
Anyone know how to do that?  See:

   http://stackoverflow.com/questions/6674795/how-to-call-generic-template-function-in-a-specialization-version

So I think that's going to make testing really painful, too, because
it'll require copying the template definition into new name for testing
against the specialization.

If that's still not clear, I can write the exp() specialization for
fvar<fvar<var> > and test it.  Daniel, if I do that, where do you think
it should go --- we have agrad/fwd and agrad/rev, so I'm thinking
agrad/fwd_rev and agrad/fwd_rev_rev respectively.

- Bob

messages.subject: vector-based fwd-mode auto-diff
messages.body_plain:
Probably the best thing we could do to speed up
Hessian calcs is to use a vector-based forward mode
that computes multiple forward derivatives at once.
Right now, our Hessian calculation works for a K-dimensional
input by running fvar<var> K times, each of which calculates
a gradient of a single partial (a row of the Hessian matrix).

Now:

   fvar<T> {
     T val_;  // value
     T d_;    // tangent w.r.t. single input
     ...
   }

With vectors:

   fvar_vec<T> {
     T val_;                   // value
     Matrix<T,Dynamic,1> ds_;  // tangent w.r.t. multiple inputs

     fvar(T& val, Matrix<T,Dynamic,1>& ds) : val_(val), ds_(ds) { }
   }

For instance, exp() will look like this:

   template <typename T>
   inline
   fvar_vec<T>
   exp(const fvar_vec<T>& x) {
     T val = exp(x.val_);
     return fvar_vec<T>(val, val * x.ds_);
   }

Presumably the overhead of dealing with vectors will be
less than repeated evals of exp().  In general, the biggest gains
will be with higher dimensionality [fewer allocations per item] and
more complex functions [more expensive computations eliminated], which
is just what we want to speed up.

We are going to have mixed operations (fvar_vec and double), for which
we'd need to specialize the matrix operators like * one more time to
allow clean fvar_vec implementations.

Hessians are now a single evaluation of fvar_vec<var> with a dimension
of ds equal to the number of parameters.

The new C++11 construct-on-collection operators for std::vector<T>
might be more efficient and outweigh the convenience of doing vector
arithmetic in Eigen.

Unfortunately, this would require an entirely new set of fvar_vec
implementations.   The good news is that they're all just vectorized
versions of what we already have.  And we can use the non-vector versions
for testing.

Of course, we could also unfold the higher-order derivatives in this
situation, but I can't bear to think of the bookkeeping.

- Bob

messages.subject: Changing how groups of tests run
messages.subject_clean: Changing how groups of tests run
messages.body_plain:
Would anyone be opposed to changing how groups of tests currently run? Here is what I propose:

To run any tests in a subdirectory, use that subdirectory as a target. For example, to run all the tests in src/test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians, it would look like:
    make src/test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians

This would run the three tests in that folder:
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/dense_e_metric
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/diag_e_metric
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/unit_e_metric

If you ran it from a folder one level up, like:
    make src/test/mcmc/hmc

It would run these tests:
  - test/mcmc/hmc/base_hmc
  - test/mcmc/hmc/base_nuts
  - test/mcmc/hmc/base_static_hmc
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/dense_e_metric
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/diag_e_metric
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/unit_e_metric
  - test/mcmc/hmc/hamiltonians/unit_e_metric

messages.body_plain:
I verified that this is a bug in 2.0.1.   I also verified
that our current development branch (what will soon be 2.1.0)
does NOT have this problem.

We need to write to our user's list ASAP about what's going on.
Does someone other than me want to do this?

Clearly N_eff and R_hat aren't enough for diagnosing problems
like these.

It's very worrisome that we haven't been more careful testing
posterior variance estimates.   We need to add this as a test
case before 2.1.0 hits the streets.

Here are the answers I get with Andrew's model (b1 and b2
both unit normal).

CmdStan 2.0.1, default adaptation:

- Bob

> Hi, all.  This is the problem that I was having the other day, I stripped down the model and stripped it down and stripped it down until I came up with the following two examples.  I can't figure out what is going on!  It's the simplest Gaussian model, it works fine in one dimension but not in two dimensions.  I don't know if it's a bug in Stan, or in Nuts, or something stupid I'm doing, or what???  I'm doing 20,000 iterations so I don't think it is a convergence issue.

> A

>

> R script:
>
> library ("rstan")

> sims <- extract(gaussian1)$b1
> print (mean (sims))
> print (var (sims))
> gaussian2 <- stan (file="gaussian2.stan", iter=20000, chains=4)
> sims <- extract(gaussian2)$b1
> print (mean (sims))
> print (var (sims))

>> sims <- extract(gaussian1)$b1

> [1] 0.006627426

But the univariate is OK.  This is what made me worry that there's some sort of Nuts problem.  But I have no idea.  Maybe it is some implicit constraint happening within Stan?  Or something else?  I also noticed the problem when b was a vector; I expressed it above as two scalars (b1 and b2) just to make sure that vectorization wasn't the problem.

messages.body_plain:
This doesn't make any sense -- the only real difference was a tweak in how the average
acceptance probability (and hence step size) was being calculated.  But the fact that
increasing the average acceptance probability makes the problem worse goes in the
wrong direction.

The median is correct and the distribution is appropriately symmetric.  The only thought
I have is that the integrator might have been diverging past 1.5 sigma, but in that case
increasing the target acceptance probability (and decreasing the step size) would help.
And increasing the dimensionality by one wouldn't have any big effect.

I'll look into it.

messages.subject: Autodiff Methods
messages.body_plain:
Bob,

Currently there's a big difference between calling first-order and higher-order autodiff.

First-order autodiff (i.e. gradients) are called using grad_log_prob defined in src/stan/model/util.hpp,

    double log_prob_grad(const M& model,
                         Eigen::VectorXd& params_r,
                         Eigen::VectorXd& gradient,
                         std::ostream* msgs = 0)

Higher-order autodiff, however, are all called using functionals defined in src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp, for example

    grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
                 const F& f,
                 const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
                 const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& M,
                 Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH)

>From an API perspective the former is much nicer as it avoids having to create a functional to wrap models
-- why wasn't this pattern repeated for the higher-order methods?

At the very least it would be much less confusing if the patterns were unified.  I'm guessing a move to functions everywhere,
in which case I'd much prefer to define a generic functional as well as wrappers to the autodiff code that take in a model
to hide the call to the functional.

> Bob,

>
> First-order autodiff (i.e. gradients) are called using grad_log_prob defined in src/stan/model/util.hpp,
>
>      double log_prob_grad(const M& model,
>                           Eigen::VectorXd& params_r,
>                           Eigen::VectorXd& gradient,
>                           std::ostream* msgs = 0)
>
> Higher-order autodiff, however, are all called using functionals defined in src/stan/agrad/autodiff.hpp, for example
>
>      grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
>                   const F& f,
>                   const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
>                   const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& M,
>                   Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH)
>
>  From an API perspective the former is much nicer as it avoids having to create a functional to wrap models

Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
in functions).  There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.

> -- why wasn't this pattern repeated for the higher-order methods?

I find the latter much nicer.  It's much more modular in that
the model only defines the log prob.  If I had it to do over,
I'd eliminate the log_prob_grad method from the models rather than
the other way around.

> At the very least it would be much less confusing if the patterns were unified.

Absolutely.

> I'm guessing a move to functions everywhere,

How well you know me!

We're also going to have to address compile times.  If every model or
the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
going to be slow.

> in which case I'd much prefer to define a generic functional as well as wrappers to the autodiff code that take in a model
> to hide the call to the functional.

That's how I imagined it going.  The subtlelty here is that we
need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.

The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor.  Or
you could just use the functor class directly.  Or you could just
use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.

- Bob

to compile it.

fundamental problem is that the model's templated log prob

Exactly what I had in mind for the functor.  (Please don't put an "_" before
a structure name.  We're trying to move away from initial "_", which are
technically not allowed (though tend not to cause problems other than when
followed by a single capital letter).  And I'd like to reserve suffix "_"
for member variables in classes.)

Definitely the latter.  We do not want autodiff.hpp to depend on our models
or vice-versa, so it should go in model/util.

Right.

for you:

   template <typename M>
   inline softabs_fun<M>
   as_functor(const M& m, std::ostream* out) {
     return softabs_fun<M>(m,o);
   }

It only saves you having to include the model parameter.
It'd be nice if we could do this and keep softabs_fun<M>
anonymous.  To do that, we could use bind:

What kind of tests do you want to see for these interfaces?  Just that they don't throw exceptions (for a Stan model using only simple manipulations at the moment) or actual verification of the gradients?  Or something else?

On Dec 17, 2013, at 10:27 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:

> On Tue, Dec 17, 2013 at 8:43 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Use case as in the samplers or tests?
> >
> Samplers.
>
>
> Perhaps we could have a flag for stanc that would control whether we use a higher order auto-diff or not. Then we'd include one command.hpp or similar for just HMC and another for higher order?
>
>
>
>
>
> > > On Dec 17, 2013, at 7:07 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Looks good to me (modulo naming conventions).
> > >
> > > In the use case, I think at least one of the log_prob
> > > calls should get the error messages turned on, but they
> > > don't all need to be turned on.
> > >
> > > - Bob
> > >
> > >
> > >> On 12/17/13, 6:13 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > >> How about this going into model/util.hpp:
> > >>
> > >>     template <typename M>
> > >>     struct _softabs_fun {
> > >>
> > >>       const M& _model;
> > >>       std::ostream* _o;
> > >>
> > >>       _softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};
> > >>
> > >>       template <typename T>
> > >>       T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
> > >>         return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
> > >>       }
> > >>
> > >>     };
> > >>
> > >>     template <class M>
> > >>     stan::model::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(
> > >>                  const M& model,
> > >>                  const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x,
> > >>                  const Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,Eigen::Dynamic>& X,
> > >>                  Eigen::Matrix<double,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& grad_tr_MH,
> > >>                  std::ostream* msgs = 0) {
> > >>
> > >>         stan::agrad::grad_tr_mat_times_hessian(_softabs_fun<M>(model, msgs), x, X, grad_tr_MH);
> > >>
> > >>     }
> > >>
> > >> with better names, etc (although I hate using a suffix _ to denote members -- it's incredibly easy to miss.
> > >> I always liked the m/f prefix, but that was for CamelCase).
> > >>
> > >> We can also add the intermediate for type inference, but I can't see a strong argument
> > >> for adding it at the moment.
> > >>
> > >>> On Dec 17, 2013, at 5:57 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> > >>>
> > >>>
> > >>>
> > >>> On 12/17/13, 5:00 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > >>>>> Terminologically in C++, a "functional" is something that takes functions
> > >>>>> as arguments., whereas a "functor" is a class that defines a function.
> > >>>>> So in the above, grad_tr_mat_times_hessian is a functional, and the
> > >>>>> f passed in is a functor (though it'll also accept other ways of passing
> > >>>>> in functions).  There's a very nice discussion in Vandevoorde and Josuttis.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> I can never remember the order -- especially given the definitions in math.
> > >>>
> > >>> I first learned the word in Lisp, then in category theory, and
> > >>> only after that in C++.  Language gets awfully overloaded.
> > >>>
> > >>> Wikipedia doesn't agree with my definition of "functional", redirecting
> > >>> to:
> > >>>
> > >>>  http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functor_(C%2B%2B)
> > >>>
> > >>>>> We're also going to have to address compile times.  If every model or
> > >>>>> the command winds up having to compile the model for all types, it's
> > >>>>> going to be slow.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> Can we just split up the autodiff.hpp into first, second, and third order files?
> > >>>> Then we'd only include and build what we need.
> > >>>
> > >>> autodiff.hpp isn't the issue.  It's that we have to make
> > >>> a compile-time decision about what to build.  So if there's
> > >>> an option in the compiled command to use third order, we need
> > >>> to compile it.
> > >>>
> > >>> I haven't figured out how to get around this issue.  The
> > >>> fundamental problem is that the model's templated log prob
> > >>> function has to get instantiated at compile time in all the
> > >>> ways it might be used at run time.
> > >>>
> > >>>>> That's how I imagined it going.  The subtlelty here is that we
> > >>>>> need to bind the print stream and functionally abstract (in the
> > >>>>> lambda function sense) on the parameter vector.
> > >>>>>
> > >>>>> The most abstracted way to do this would be with factory function
> > >>>>> that mapped a const model pointer and ostream to a functor.  Or
> > >>>>> you could just use the functor class directly.  Or you could just
> > >>>>> use bind or one of its generalizations in Boost.
> > >>>>
> > >>>> I've been doing this,
> > >>>>
> > >>>>     template <typename M>
> > >>>>     struct _softabs_fun {
> > >>>>
> > >>>>       const M& _model;
> > >>>>       std::ostream* _o;
> > >>>>
> > >>>>       _softabs_fun(M& m, std::ostream* out): _model(m), _o(out) {};
> > >>>
> > >>> M& should be const here.
> > >>>
> > >>>>       template <typename T>
> > >>>>       T operator()(Eigen::Matrix<T,Eigen::Dynamic,1>& x) const {
> > >>>>         return _model.template log_prob<true, true, T>(x, _o);
> > >>>>       }
> > >>>>
> > >>>>     };
> > >>>
> > >>> Exactly what I had in mind for the functor.  (Please don't put an "_" before
> > >>> a structure name.  We're trying to move away from initial "_", which are
> > >>> technically not allowed (though tend not to cause problems other than when
> > >>> followed by a single capital letter).  And I'd like to reserve suffix "_"
> > >>> for member variables in classes.)
> > >>>
> > >>>> which is readily thrown somewhere in autodiff or model/util, depending
> > >>>> on which way we want the dependency to go (probably the latter?).
> > >>>
> > >>> Definitely the latter.  We do not want autodiff.hpp to depend on our models
> > >>> or vice-versa, so it should go in model/util.
> > >>>
> > >>>> Then the wrappers would just be calling the functor.
> > >>>
> > >>> Right.
> > >>>
> > >>> What I was suggesting is a factory function that does the type inference
> > >>> for you:
> > >>>
> > >>>  template <typename M>
> > >>>  inline softabs_fun<M>
> > >>>  as_functor(const M& m, std::ostream* out) {
> > >>>    return softabs_fun<M>(m,o);
> > >>>  }
> > >>>
> > >>> It only saves you having to include the model parameter.
> > >>> It'd be nice if we could do this and keep softabs_fun<M>
> > >>> anonymous.  To do that, we could use bind:
> > >>>
> > >>>  http://www.cplusplus.com/reference/functional/bind/
> > >>>
> > >>> I like how they documented the return type!
> > >>>
> > >>>
> > >>> - Bob
> > >>>
