messages.body_plain:
I just build rstan with R 3.0.1 and got (from make build in the
rstan/rstan directory)

* checking for empty or unneeded directories
Removed empty directory ï¿½rstan/inst/include/stansrc/models/bugs_examples/vol2/biopsiesï¿½
Removed empty directory ï¿½rstan/inst/include/stansrc/models/bugs_examples/vol3/jamaï¿½
* adding MD5 file
* building ï¿½rstan_2.0.1.tar.gzï¿½
Warning in utils::tar(filepath, pkgname, compression = "gzip", compression_level = 9L,  :
   storing paths of more than 100 bytes is not portable:
   ï¿½rstan/inst/include/stanlib/boost_1.54.0/boost/accumulators/framework/accumulators/droppable_accumulator.hppï¿½
Warning in utils::tar(filepath, pkgname, compression = "gzip", compression_level = 9L,  :
   storing paths of more than 100 bytes is not portable:

and many more warnings about the path length.

I'm guessing this is a new check added by R, since I didn't see it with
R 2.15.1.

I'm assuming since I have gnu utilities (Debian) this is not actually an
issue for me; I just thought I'd report it here.

Ross Boylan

messages.subject: r?stan: odd change
messages.body_plain:
I just reran a calculation I did first on Oct 9 in rstan and got a much
different (better) n_eff.  In both cases I was working off the
development branch.  Have there been any changes that might account for
it?

The division between warmup and sampling is also much different (much
more warmup time in the old version).  At least according the the R help
for stan() the warmup and delta defaults have not changed (and the
maximum n_eff is 100 = 1/2 requested iterations for both).

A spot check of the actual coefficient estimates shows they are similar
between the old and new runs.

Of course, I may not actually be making the same request.

The old version is R 2.15; the new is R 3.01.  If the same seed produces
different random numbers (though I guess it's really in stan that that
happens) it might account for the difference.  The runs are also on
different machines in different software environments.

Also, I just realized I am not doing set.seed() in R. I don't think the
call uses R's random numbers.

Old:

+                       iter=200, chains=1))

I can share the model but not the data.  It's clustered multinomial.
data {
   int<lower=0> N; // number of partners
   int<lower=2> K; // number of types of partner race
       // K is the number of categories in the outcome pEthnic
   int<lower=0> J;  //number of covariates
   int<lower=0> NSD;  // number of classes of beta for sd
   int<lower=1,upper=NSD> SDClass[J];  // beta[j, k] has
sigma_beta[SDClass[j]]
   int<lower=1,upper=K> pEthnic[N];  // partner race
   int<lower=0> NCLUSTER;  //number of respondents
   int iCluster[N]; // cluster id
   row_vector[J] x[N];  // covariates
}
parameters {
    matrix[J, K] beta_raw; // standard covariate coefficients
    vector[K] alpha_raw[NCLUSTER]; // cluster effects
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0> sigma_beta[NSD];
    //vector<lower=0>[NSD] df; // df for t distn
}
transformed parameters {
    matrix [J, K] beta;
    vector[K] alpha[NCLUSTER];
    for(ir in 1:J)
       beta[ir] <- beta_raw[ir]*sigma_beta[SDClass[ir]];
    for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
      alpha[i] <- alpha_raw[i]*sigma;
}
model {
    vector[K] beta_x;
    sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    sigma_beta ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    //df ~ cauchy(0, 5);
    for(ir in 1:J)
       beta_raw[ir] ~ normal(0, 1); //or student_t(df[SDClass[ir]], 0,
1);
    for(i in 1:NCLUSTER)
      alpha_raw[i] ~ normal(0, 1);
    for(n in 1:N) {
      beta_x <- (x[n] * beta)'+alpha[iCluster[n]];
      pEthnic[n] ~ categorical_logit(beta_x);
    }
}
>
> dim(x) # summary of results.  I.e., 7915 parameters
[1] 7915   10
> dim(mm)  # this is the covariate matrix above
[1] 1755   97

Note that many parameters come in pairs, raw and transformed.

Ross Boylan

messages.body_plain:
Let me start by saying that it's great people are volunteering
to contribute code at all.  I really appreciate what Marcus is
doing to help.

I'm sympathetic to both sides of this discussion.

I'm not convinced we need to test every private helper function
we use.  I'd rather put energy into properly specifying and
testing the higher-level functions that are actually exposed.

Also, if we start enforcing rules at the syntactic level like every
function needs a test, our developers, being good problem solvers,
might start wiggling around the intent by cutting-and-pasting code into
monolithic functions to cut down on unit-testing requirements.

At the same time, I'm fully behind the practice of writing code
modularly enough that functions can be documented and hence
tested.  Documentability is a precondition for testability, because
we need to understand the intent of a function to test it.

These particular functions are important and complicated, so it's perhaps
not surprising they're causing some level of frustration with
testing and integration.   I think part of the problem is that neither
Daniel nor I are comfortable enough with all of these matrix operations
to understand what's intended by looking at the code;  this is why we're
worried about maintainability.

A middle ground would be to add some doc on what they're supposed
to do and how to test them.  I'm willing to help write the tests if
I can understand what they're supposed to be.

I'm probably the most guilty of all of us by not unit testing and
documenting the parser.  I really do hope to shore it up after 2.1.0 is
out, but other more pressing issues keep coming up.  The lack of testing
is what's blocking some changes to the parser I'd like to make and
also blocking Robert Goedman's pull request for C++11 compatibility.
So I feel Marcus's frustration firsthand as well.

- Bob

On 12/19/13, 10:45 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> @mbrubake, I understand your distinction between public API vs private API,
> but that isn't a reason to not test something.
>
> I'm asking to add unit tests to LDLT_alloc for a few reasons:
> - it's hard to instantiate. Having a unit test showing the next developer
> how to instantiate it would cut down hours of work just figuring out how to
> call it directly.
> - it does a lot of work. Lots of things depend on it. I would feel much
> more comfortable if it was tested.
> - if I'm looking at just the class, how am I to know what compute() or
> log_abs_det() do, what the valid values of its arguments are, and if it is
> even safe to call?
>
> My motivation for having tests in is to save time for the next person that
> has to touch the code. If existed an example test that instantiated the
> class in a standalone test that, in and of itself, saves a lot of time.
> Knowing how to call each of the functions saves a whole lot more. Given
> that the class isn't well documented (and I'm not asking you to document
> it), the minimal amount of courtesy you can provide to the next person that
> has to look at this code is to provide some documentation on how to use it
> and a little bit of code that shows that it doesn't crash.
>
> If you're having trouble creating tests, then there's a problem with the
> design of the code. If you're not creating unit tests out of principle,
> someone else will need to write tests before the pull request gets in.
>
> It'll take you a lot less time to write 3 tests (one for the constructor,
> one for compute(), one for log_abs_det()), than it will take for anyone
> else to write those three tests. I've already sunk a lot of time into
> breaking everything apart and testing the rest of the untested,
> undocumented functions, so please return the courtesy and write 3 tests.
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
[back on stan-dev]

The context is structured matrices and having a special
case for zero in matrix multiplication to get rid of
the big expression trees in sparse matrices.  More below.

On 12/20/13, 4:14 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On 12/20/2013 04:11 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>> On 12/20/13, 4:05 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
>> ...
>>> Yeah, also what do people think of having the multiplication and
>>> division operations check to see if we are multiplying
>>> by exactly zero. It would slow things down a bit but might be offset
>>> by avoiding the autodiff.
>>
>> You mean multiplying by a double that's exactly zero?  We could do
>> that, but I think it'll be a huge slowdown for the usual cases.
>
> That's what I meant. Maybe it should be a compile-option that is off by default, like -DDONTMULTIPLYBYZERO? You could
> even avoid multiplying by a zero var as long as the user knew to avoid initializing the parameters to zero.

That's an interesting idea.  We just have to make sure
everything's testable and documentable for users.  If
there are too many switches for them to set, it gets confusing.
And one is too many for most of us!  But presumably doing something
just for this kind of modeling would be easier to manage.

I also think the ramifications are different once we start
computing Hessians --- there are going to be many more zeroes
if we do it the way we're doing now, which is computing an
N x N Hessian by running N passes where parameters are fvar<var>,
but all the tangents (derivative of fvar) are 0 but one.  If
we move to vector-based derivatives, that's different again.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
There's no reason in principle to synchronize releases.
But I do think it's easier on our users that way, most of
whom are going to be using either RStan or PyStan.

So I'd like to keep our releases synched until it becomes
too much of a burden.  Releasing CmdStan ahead of RStan/PyStan
just doesn't buy us much.

Anyone else have a preference?

The current plan is to break out CmdStan from Stan in the same
way as RStan or PyStan.  Hopefully that'll be done by 2.2.  Then
the drill will be to stabilize Stan, then update CmdStan,
RStan and PyStan.  If we get more organized in the design of
Stan itself (also a target for 2.2), we can provide a reliable
warning of when the underlying Stan interface is stable so that
RStan/PyStan dev can work from there rather than waiting for
CmdStan/Stan to have ribbons on them.

- Bob

in place to evaluate fvar expression templates, so just an inlined
function.  It might be worth thinking about moving to expression
templates.

I was thinking of something like operators and partials only more
lightweight and with a fixed number of pre-built derivatives.

On 12/22/13, 12:37 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> Let me rephrase my question -- why does the fvar<fvar<var> specialization just
> create and then fill the fvar<var> and not the value/adjoint of the four underlying vars?
> It is straightforward to compute everything for the vars -- is there an autodiff limitation?

You need an underlying vari class for the four underlying
vars.  Given that, you can fill in whatever you want.
In my example, all four vari were computed at once and then
built out and returned.  I like to think of it this way:

   exp([(a,b),(c,d)] = [(e,f),(g,h)]

Each of the a,b,c,d are input var (underlyingly the vari is
what matters) and e,f,g,h are output vars.

In code, the general pattern is this:

    inline fvar<fvar<var> >
    exp(const fvar<fvar<var> >& x) {
      var a = x.val_.val_;
      var b = x.val_.d_;
      var c = x.d_.val_;
      var d = x.d_.val_;

      var e = ...
      var f = ...
      var g = ...
      var h = ...
      return fvar<fvar<var> >(fvar<var>(e,f),
                              fvar<var>(g,h));
    }

If you create a vari class that generally just holds the
adjoint value and the pointer to the vari input, then you
can do all the calculations in each class and then just return
instances of the is vari class (wrapped in var) for each of
the four var that make up an fvar<fvar<var> >.

If you want to instead rethink fvar<fvar<var> > as not being
compounded out of four var, that's a different issue.  I'm sure
there'd be some way to do it, but you lose the automatic
implementation.  As is, we get the fvar<fvar<T>> for free through
the implementation of fvar<S> (not exactly for free --- everything
has to be templated enough in the implementation to let fvar<T>
be plugged in for S and var for T).

- Bob

expression tree for each of the four vari that you
produce, you can use agrad::precomp_v_vari from:

   agrad/rev/internal/precomp_v_vari.hpp

The constructor takes the value, the vari to which
the derivative will be propagated, and the partial.

If you look at binary operations like multiplication (*),
you'll find you need more than eight doubles.  You have
8 var coming in and you need 4 going out, so the ones going
out need a bit more connectivity.

- Bob

messages.subject: Stan 2.1.0 ASAP, other improvements later?
messages.body_plain:
I'd like to get 2.1.0 out the door ASAP because of
the bug in variance estimation in 2.0.1.

I believe CmdStan 2.1.0 is all ready to go (Daniel, is that right?).

I'd like to get a 2.1.0 release of RStan/PyStan out ASAP,
even if it means holding off some important features until
2.1.0.1.  Is there an estimate of how long this will take and
whether it's feasible?

Andrew wanted to delay announcing the bug to the users because
we don't have 2.1.0 ready.  Everyone seemed to think we should announce
2.1.0 for all platforms at the same time.

This is making me very uneasy and I don't think it's fair to our
users.  If we can't get PyStan and RStan 2.1.0 out soon, my own preference
is to announce the bug with an example, release CmdStan 2.1.0, and tell
users to stop using Stan until 2.1.0 comes out or to go back to 1.3.0,
which didn't have this bug.

Sorry the timing is so bad w.r.t. the holidays.  This wouldn't be
so urgent if we hadn't found the critical bug in the sampler in
2.0.1.

- Bob

messages.subject: (R/Py/Cmd)Stan 2.1.0
messages.body_plain:
We're happy to announce the release of Stan C++, CmdStan,
RStan, and PyStan 2.1.0.  This is a minor feature release,
but it is also an important bug fix release.  As always, the
place to start is the (all new) Stan web pages:

  http://mc-stan.org/

Major Bug in 2.0.0, 2.0.1
------------------------------
Stan 2.0.0 and Stan 2.0.1 introduced a bug in the implementation
of the NUTS criterion that led to poor tail exploration and
thus biased the posterior uncertainty downward.  There was no
bug in NUTS in Stan 1.3 or earlier, and 2.1 has been extensively tested
and tests put in place so this problem will not recur.

If you are using Stan 2.0.0 or 2.0.1, you should switch to 2.1.0 as
soon as possible and rerun any models you care about.

New Target Acceptance Rate Default for Stan 2.1.0
------------------------------
Another big change aimed at reducing posterior estimation bias
was an increase in the target acceptance rate during adaptation
from 0.65 to 0.80.  The bad news is that iterations will take
around 50% longer because of the reduced step size required to
achieve the higher acceptance rate.  The good news is that chains
should be less variable and tails of hierarchical models should
be explored more efficiently (in particular, fewer "stuck" chains).

There are also new configuration parameters that let you control how
long the various phases of adaptation last, with explanations in the
command section of the manual.

The change was motivated by:

    M. J. Betancourt, Mark Girolami.  2013.
    Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Models.
    http://arxiv.org/abs/1312.0906

New Features and Minor Bug Fixes
------------------------------
The full list can be found in the release notes at:

    https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/releases/tag/v2.1.0

The highlights in addition to adaptation are a switch to BFGS
as the default optimizer (about an order of magnitude faster and
also more stable), fixes to bugs in bin/print for CmdStan for
matrices, bug fixes to multi_normal_prec(), bernoulli(), bernoulli_logit(),
and Phi(), sd(), var(), all of which are now more stable for vectorization and
arithmetic (former bugs caused crashes, not wrong answers).  Windows
now builds in 64-bit mode, and g++ 4.4 now works.  There were also many
updates to clarify the manual.

As always, we'd love to hear from you on our mailing lists if
you have suggestions, bug reports, problems installing, etc.

- Stan Development Team

messages.subject: a Waic example!
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.  I've programmed a simple example of WAIC for the example on p.165 and p.177 of BDA3.  Attached are three files:
waic_example.R
lm_waic.stan
hibbs.dat

I have some thoughts on how we could alter Stan to do this automatically.  The simplest approach would be to just put a function waic() in rstan that looks in the output for the variable "log_lik" and, if such a variable exists, calculates Waic.  A more comprehensive approach would allow tagging of the Stan model so that certain lines of code would be identified with the loglikelihood so that "log_lik" would get calculated automatically.

By the way:  in calculating Waic, we do want to use the full loglik (including the normalizing factor); this gets done automatically when we use increment_log_prob in Stan. If we did it using tagging, we'd just have to be sure to remember to include those factors.

---

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stochastic linear regression based VB
messages.body_plain:
Unless I misunderstood something, all they're doing is using a single-sample Monte Carlo estimate to compute the variational expectations needed for updating the variational parameters.  When using variational distributions for the exponential family they show that this Monte Carlo approximation is equivalent to a kind of stochastic VB.

Personally I find the appeal of stochastic VB to be the ability to stream data and, although they note the possibility of extending their algorithm to admit such a feature, it is not a fundamental part if their approach.  I dunno, at some level it seems like a Cache-22 - yes, you can get better variational approximations by using richer variational distributions but then you have to model twice, once for the actual model and once for its approximation.

messages.subject: the appeal of stochastic vb?
messages.body_plain:
M

I agree that settings with streaming data are a natural for stochastic optimization algorithms of all kinds, but I thought there was another important application area of stochastic VB, even in non-streaming, fixed data examples.  I'm thinking, for example, of hierarchical models with, say, 10^5 data points and 10^3 groups, maybe some varying intercepts and slopes, so that straight HMC (or, worse, Metropolis) could be fairly slow, taking 20 minutes or so.  Instead it would be great to have a black-box VB algorithm, and I could imagine stochastic approximation as being part of that story.

I guess what I'm saying is:  right now we do not have any black-box distributional approximation that runs in Stan.  As we stand, all we have is HMC (or joint optimization, which is essentially useless for the sorts of problems I'm thinking about).  I think if we had any black box implementation of a distributional approximation, then we could talk about strengths and weaknesses of alternatives.  But, given that we have nuthin, anything looks good to me!

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] stochastic linear regression based VB
messages.body_plain:
My understanding (very rough given my lack of depth in VB, KL, and
exponential families) from the paper was that they were suggesting
an approach to non-conjugate models based on an exponential family
approximation.  This approximation would be exact in some conjugate
exponential family models and provide a more generalized Laplace-type
approximation elsewhere.  I didn't see any automatic way to exploit
the extra generality --- I think this is what Michael was saying when
he said you'd have to model twice.

They also have a bunch of different approaches to implementation
from batch to mini-batch (the latter of which does seem stochastic);
I didn't follow the distinctions very closely and I don't know the
history of all these algorithms for VB.

I agree that it would be nice to have something that's general, even if
it's not stochastic.  If it were stochastic, that'd be awesome.  I'll
be happy to let you all sort out the academic provenance of the ideas.

- Bob

P.S.  I like the idea of a "Cache 22".  It would only let you
read a value if it's already in the cache.

Yeah, Bob definitely echoed my sentiments.

The problem with VB is that it requires a second step in defining the variational distributions.  This is why there are so many different variations (hah!) of the algorithm out there.

I think what Andrew wants is a choice of variational distribution that works okay for all models - I think the Laplace or delta algorithms are the best choice here (once we have efficient higher-order autodiff these will be easy to implement).

VB, however, also lets us enter the world of big data (yes, I hate myself for saying that).  This requires not just generic VB but also the ability to stream batches, which is what the original stochastic VB buys you.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] the appeal of stochastic vb?
messages.body_plain:
The issue here is that the hyperparameters marginals are highly skewed and often heavy-tailed. This pushes typical variational distributions (like the Gaussian) beyond what would be considered a reasonable approximation.  What would be really great would be Student variational distributions, but that makes the math explode.

There will definitely be two modeling steps here (this is the huge benefit of MCMC, which works for any model).  The question is whether or not we do the second step or we force the user to do it.

messages.subject: implementing waic
messages.body_plain:
We could do Waic in rstan as is (just using the function I already wrote!), conditional on the user creating the log_lik vector correctly in the Stan program.  But maybe it makes sense to get it working in regular Stan using tagging.  That sort of user intervention (tagging lines in the model as components in the loglik vector) would be necessary in any case.  There's no way that it could be done automatically given only the log posterior function with no labeling.

I do think, however, that we should be able to do it without setting up intermediate log probability variables.  I think it should be possible (at least for many many common examples) to just have the user tag the appropriate lines in the model as being log-likleihood terms.

A

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] the appeal of stochastic vb?
messages.body_plain:
On Saturday, December 28, 2013 4:54:55 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> The issue here is that the hyperparameters marginals are highly skewed and often heavy-tailed. This pushes typical variational distributions (like the Gaussian) beyond what would be considered a reasonable approximation.  What would be really great would be Student variational distributions, but that makes the math explode.

Not here; their method extends to mixtures of exponential family distributions. Have a look at their final example (the beta-binomial). They use a discrete mixture, but a continuous mixture like the t would be a straightforward extension. You start with a model p(y, theta) that you would like to approximate with a family q(theta), where q(theta) = \int q(theta, u) du. If your model is p(y, theta) you augment to the model p(y, theta, u) = p(y, theta)q(u|theta) and proceed with the variational distribution q(theta, u) which is now tractable. This problem has the same optima as the original problem with p(y, theta) and q(theta), I believe.  The preceding section where they describe using triangular q's (i.e. q(theta_1)q(theta_2 | theta_1) ) is also interesting.

I don't know whether these tricks are standard in the VB literature but they seem very important to me. Fixed form VB has at least a chance of capturing complex dependence, particularly when you can go beyond the exponential family. Mean field methods have been effective but a factorized approximate posterior just isn't going to work for a lot of applications, including most of mine.

I've got no connection to the Knowles & Salimans paper but I hope stan-dev will take a hard look. Stan has the modeling language to express both the true model and perhaps the approximate posterior *and* Stan has the AD (their methods can use gradients and Hessians where they're available).

>
>
>
> There will definitely be two modeling steps here (this is the huge benefit of MCMC, which works for any model).  The question is whether or not we do the second step or we force the user to do it.
>
>
>
> > On Dec 28, 2013, at 4:46 PM, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> >
>
> >
>
> >
>
> >> On 12/28/13, 4:40 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
>
> >> Sure, I just meant that I don't think this offers anything more than what Dave, his students, and I are working on.
>
> >>  Incidentally, the hyperparameters in hierarchical models have marginal distributions that are sufficiently wacky to
>
> >> render most variational distributions poor approximations.  I think this is one of the reasons I've been having such a
>
> >> hard time with the current algorithm.
>
> >
>
> > Is it the general form of the approximations, the variable-at-a-time
>
> > nature of the approximations, or both?
>
> >
>
> > Seems like we'll have to go down the rabbit hole of double modeling,
>
> > be it automatic or manual.
>
> >
>
> > - Bob
